paragraphs: When he was halfway there, the sharp dry wind that had blown early that morning rose again, and a fine dry snow began to fall thickly. It did not settle on the ground but whirled around in the wind, and soon it was a regular snowstorm. There were hardly any lamp-posts in the part of town where Smerdyakov lived. Ivan strode on alone in the dark, not noticing the storm, picking his way by instinct. His head ached and his temples throbbed painfully. He could feel his hands twitching convulsively. Not far from Marya Kondratyevna’s cottage, Ivan suddenly came upon a lone, drunken little peasant. He wore a coarse, patched coat and walked in zigzags, grumbling and swearing to himself. Then all at once he would start singing in a husky, drunken voice:
“Ach, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg; I won’t wait till he comes back.”

But each time he broke off after the second line and started swearing again, and then he would begin the same song over. Ivan felt a fierce hatred for him before he had even thought about him. Then he suddenly became aware of the man and felt an irresistible urge to knock him down. Just then they met, and the peasant lurched violently and fell headlong against Ivan, who shoved him back in a fury. The peasant went flying backwards and dropped like a log on the frozen ground. He gave one plaintive “O—oh!” and then fell silent. Ivan stepped up to him. He lay on his back, without moving or any sign of consciousness. “He’ll freeze,” thought Ivan, and he went on his way to Smerdyakov’s.

In the passage, Marya Kondratyevna, who had run out to open the door with a candle in her hand, whispered that Smerdyakov was very ill. “It’s not that he’s laid up, but he doesn’t seem himself, and he even told us to take the tea away. He wouldn’t have any.”
“What, does he make a row?” asked Ivan coarsely.
“Oh, dear, no, quite the opposite, he’s very quiet. Only please don’t talk to him too long,” Marya Kondratyevna begged him. Ivan opened the door and stepped into the room.

It was overheated, as before, but the room had changed. One of the benches along the wall had been taken out, and in its place stood a large old mahogany sofa covered in leather, with a bed made up on it, with fairly clean white pillows. Smerdyakov was sitting on the sofa in the same dressing-gown. The table had been pulled out in front of the sofa, so there was hardly room to move. On the table lay a thick book in a yellow cover, but Smerdyakov was not reading it. He seemed to be sitting there doing nothing. He met Ivan with a slow, silent stare and did not seem at all surprised that he had come. His face was greatly changed. He was much thinner and sallower. His eyes were sunken, with blue marks under them.
“Why, you really are ill?” Ivan stopped short. “I won’t keep you long. I won’t even take off my coat. Where can a man sit down?”
He went to the other end of the table, pulled up a chair and sat down.
“Why do you look at me and say nothing? I’ve come with just one question, and I swear I won’t leave without an answer. Has the young lady, Katerina Ivanovna, been to see you?”
Smerdyakov still said nothing, looking quietly at Ivan as before. Suddenly he waved his hand and turned his face away.
“What’s the matter with you?” cried Ivan.
“Nothing.”
“What do you mean, ‘nothing’?”
“Yes, she has. It’s no business of yours. Leave me alone.”
“No, I won’t leave you alone. Tell me, when was she here?”

“Why, I’d completely forgotten about her,” said Smerdyakov with a scornful smile. Turning his face to Ivan again, he stared at him with a look of frenzied hatred, the same look he had fixed on him at their last interview, a month before.
“You look very ill yourself. Your face is sunken. You don’t look like yourself,” he said to Ivan.
“Never mind my health. Tell me what I’m asking you.”
“But why are your eyes so yellow? The whites are completely yellow. Are you so worried?” He smiled contemptuously and suddenly burst out laughing.
“Listen! I told you I won’t go away without an answer!” Ivan cried, intensely irritated.
“Why do you keep pestering me? Why do you torment me?” said Smerdyakov, with a look of suffering.
“Damn it! I’ve nothing to do with you. Just answer my question and I’ll go.”
“I’ve no answer to give you,” said Smerdyakov, looking down again.
“You can be sure I’ll make you answer!”

“Why are you so uneasy?” Smerdyakov stared at him, not just with contempt but almost with disgust. “Is it because the trial begins tomorrow? Nothing will happen to you. Can’t you believe that by now? Go home, go to bed and sleep in peace. Don’t be afraid of anything.”

“I don’t understand you.... What have I got to be afraid of tomorrow?” Ivan said in astonishment, and suddenly a chill breath of fear did in fact pass over his soul. Smerdyakov looked him up and down.
“You don’t understand?” he drawled reproachfully. “It’s strange that a sensible man should want to play such a farce!”

Ivan looked at him, unable to speak. The startling, incredibly superior tone of this man, who had once been his valet, was extraordinary in itself. He had not taken such a tone even at their last interview.

“I tell you, you’ve nothing to be afraid of. I won’t say anything about you. There’s no proof against you. Look how your hands are trembling! Why are your fingers moving like that? Go home. _You_ didn’t murder him.”
Ivan started. He remembered Alyosha.
“I know it wasn’t me,” he faltered.
“Do you?” Smerdyakov caught him up again.
Ivan jumped up and seized him by the shoulder.
“Tell me everything, you viper! Tell me everything!”
Smerdyakov was not in the least frightened. He only fixed his eyes on Ivan with insane hatred.
“Well, then, it was you who murdered him, if that’s how it is,” he whispered furiously.
Ivan sank back on his chair, as though thinking something over. He laughed spitefully.
“You mean my going away. What you were talking about last time?”
“You stood in front of me last time and understood it all, and you understand it now.”
“All I understand is that you’re mad.”

“Aren’t you tired of it? Here we are, face to face. What’s the use of going on with this farce between us? Are you still trying to throw it all on me, to my face? _You_ murdered him. You are the real murderer. I was only your instrument, your faithful servant, and I did it following your words.”
“_Did_ it? Why, did you murder him?” Ivan turned cold.
Something seemed to give way in his brain, and he shuddered all over with a cold shiver. Then Smerdyakov himself looked at him in wonder. Perhaps Ivan’s horror was so genuine that it struck him.
“You don’t mean to say you really didn’t know?” he faltered mistrustfully, looking into Ivan’s eyes with a forced smile. Ivan went on gazing at him and seemed unable to speak.
Ach, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg; I won’t wait till he comes back,
suddenly echoed in his head.
“Do you know, I’m afraid you’re a dream, a phantom sitting in front of me,” he muttered.
“There’s no phantom here, only the two of us and one other. No doubt he’s here, that third, between us.”
“Who is he? Who’s here? What third person?” Ivan cried in alarm, looking around, his eyes hastily searching every corner.
“That third is God Himself—Providence. He is the third beside us now. Only don’t look for Him. You won’t find Him.”
“It’s a lie that you killed him!” Ivan cried madly. “You’re mad, or teasing me again!”

Smerdyakov, as before, watched him curiously, with no sign of fear. He could still hardly get over his disbelief. He still imagined that Ivan knew everything and was trying to “throw it all on him, to his face.”

“Wait a minute,” he said at last in a weak voice, and suddenly bringing his left leg out from under the table, he began turning up the trouser leg. He wore long white stockings and slippers. Slowly he took off his garter and fumbled down to the bottom of his stocking. Ivan gazed at him, and suddenly shuddered in a fit of terror.

“He’s mad!” he cried, and jumping up quickly, he drew back so that his back struck the wall, and he stood pressed against it, stiff and straight. He looked in insane terror at Smerdyakov, who, quite unaffected by his terror, went on fumbling in his stocking, as though he were struggling to get hold of something with his fingers and pull it out. At last he got hold of it and began pulling it out. Ivan saw that it was a piece of paper, or perhaps a roll of papers. Smerdyakov pulled it out and laid it on the table.
“Here,” he said quietly.
“What is it?” asked Ivan, trembling.
“Kindly look at it,” Smerdyakov answered, still in the same low tone.
Ivan stepped up to the table and took up the roll of paper and began to unfold it, but suddenly he snatched his fingers back, as though he had touched a loathsome reptile.
“Your hands keep twitching,” observed Smerdyakov, and he unfolded the bundle himself, taking his time. Under the wrapper were three packets of hundred-rouble notes.
“They’re all here, all three thousand roubles. You needn’t count them. Take them,” Smerdyakov suggested to Ivan, nodding at the notes. Ivan sank back in his chair. He was as white as a handkerchief.
“You frightened me ... with your stocking,” he said, with a strange grin.
“Can you really not have known until now?” Smerdyakov asked once more.
“No, I didn’t know. I kept thinking of Dmitri. Brother, brother! Ach!” He suddenly clutched his head in both hands.
“Listen. Did you kill him alone? With my brother’s help or without it?”
“It was only with you, with your help, that I killed him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch is completely innocent.”
“All right, all right. We’ll talk about me later. Why do I keep trembling? I can’t even speak properly.”

“You were bold enough then. You said ‘everything was lawful,’ and how frightened you are now,” Smerdyakov muttered in surprise. “Won’t you have some lemonade? I’ll ask for some right away. It’s very refreshing. Only I must hide this first.”

And again he motioned at the notes. He was just about to get up and call through the door to Marya Kondratyevna to make some lemonade and bring it to them. But he looked for something to cover the notes, so she wouldn’t see them. First he took out his handkerchief, and when it turned out to be very dirty, he picked up the big yellow book that Ivan had noticed on the table at the start and put it over the notes. The book was _The Sayings of the Holy Father Isaac the Syrian_. Ivan read the title mechanically.
“I won’t have any lemonade,” he said. “We’ll talk about me later. Sit down and tell me how you did it. Tell me all about it.”
“You’d better take off your greatcoat, or you’ll be too hot.” Ivan, as though he’d only just thought of it, took off his coat and, without getting up from his chair, threw it on the bench.
“Speak, please, speak.”
He seemed calmer. He waited, feeling sure that Smerdyakov would tell him _all_ about it.
“How it was done?” sighed Smerdyakov. “It was done in a most natural way, following your very words.”

“We’ll come to my words later,” Ivan broke in again, apparently quite self-possessed, speaking firmly and no longer shouting as before. “Only tell me in detail how you did it. Everything, just as it happened. Don’t forget anything. The details above all, the details, please.”
“You’d gone away, and then I fell into the cellar.”
“In a fit, or a sham one?”
“A sham one, naturally. I shammed it all. I went quietly down the steps to the very bottom and lay down quietly, and as I lay down I screamed and thrashed about, until they carried me out.”
“Wait! And were you shamming all the time afterward, and in the hospital?”
“No, not at all. The next day, in the morning, before they took me to the hospital, I had a real attack, and a worse one than I’d had for years. For two days I was completely unconscious.”
“All right, all right. Go on.”

“They laid me on the bed. I knew I’d be on the other side of the partition, because whenever I was ill, Marfa Ignatyevna used to put me there, near them. She’s always been very kind to me, from the day I was born. At night I moaned, but quietly. I kept expecting Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come.”
“Expecting him? To come to you?”

“Not to me. I expected him to come into the house, because I had no doubt he’d come that night. Being without me and getting no news, he was sure to come and climb over the fence, as he used to, and do something.”
“And if he hadn’t come?”
“Then nothing would have happened. I’d never have brought myself to it without him.”
“All right, all right ... speak more clearly, don’t hurry, and above all, don’t leave anything out!”

“I expected him to kill Fyodor Pavlovitch. I thought that was certain, because I had prepared him for it ... during the last few days.... He knew about the knocks, that was the main thing. With his suspiciousness and the fury that had been growing in him all those days, he was bound to get into the house by means of those taps. That was inevitable, so I was expecting him.”
“Wait,” Ivan interrupted. “If he had killed him, he would have taken the money and carried it off. You must have considered that. What would you have got out of it afterward? I don’t see.”

“But he would never have found the money. That was only what I told him, that the money was under the mattress. But that wasn’t true. It had been lying in a box. And afterward I suggested to Fyodor Pavlovitch, as I was the only person he trusted, that he hide the envelope with the notes in the corner behind the ikons, because no one would have guessed that place, especially if they came in a hurry. So that’s where the envelope lay, in the corner behind the ikons. It would have been absurd to keep it under the mattress. The box, at least, could be locked. But everyone believes it was under the mattress. A stupid thing to believe. So if Dmitri Fyodorovitch had committed the murder and found nothing, he would either have run away in a hurry, afraid of every sound, as always happens with murderers, or he would have been arrested. So I could always have climbed up to the ikons and taken the money away the next morning, or even that night, and it would all have been put down to Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I could count on that.”
“But what if he didn’t kill him, but only knocked him down?”

“If he didn’t kill him, of course, I wouldn’t have dared to take the money, and nothing would have happened. But I calculated that he’d beat him senseless, and I’d have time to take it then. And then I’d make out to Fyodor Pavlovitch that it was nobody but Dmitri Fyodorovitch who had taken the money after beating him.”
“Stop ... I’m getting mixed up. So it was Dmitri after all who killed him, and you only took the money?”

“No, he didn’t kill him. Well, I might as well have told you now that he was the murderer.... But I don’t want to lie to you now, because ... because if you really haven’t understood until now, as I can see for myself, and aren’t pretending, so as to throw your guilt on me to my very face, you are still responsible for it all. You knew about the murder, and you charged me to do it, and you went away knowing all about it. And so I want to prove to your face this evening that you are the only real murderer in the whole affair, and I’m not the real murderer, though I did kill him. You are the rightful murderer.”

“Why, why am I a murderer? Oh, God!” Ivan cried, unable to restrain himself at last and forgetting that he had put off discussing himself until the end of the conversation. “You still mean that Tchermashnya? Wait, tell me, why did you want my consent, if you really took Tchermashnya for consent? How will you explain that now?”

“Once I was sure of your consent, I’d have known that you wouldn’t make an outcry over those three thousand being lost, even if I’d been suspected instead of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or as his accomplice. On the contrary, you’d have protected me from others.... And when you got your inheritance, you’d have rewarded me whenever you could, for the rest of your life. For you’d have received your inheritance through me, seeing that if he had married Agrafena Alexandrovna, you wouldn’t have had a farthing.”
“Ah! So you meant to torment me for the rest of my life,” snarled Ivan. “And what if I hadn’t gone away then, but had informed against you?”

“What could you have informed? That I persuaded you to go to Tchermashnya? That’s all nonsense. Besides, after our conversation you would either have gone away or stayed. If you had stayed, nothing would have happened. I’d have known that you didn’t want it done, and I’d have attempted nothing. Since you went away, it meant you were assuring me that you wouldn’t dare inform against me at the trial, and that you’d overlook my having the three thousand. And indeed you couldn’t have prosecuted me afterward, because then I’d have told it all in court. That is, not that I had stolen the money or killed him—I wouldn’t have said that—but that you’d put me up to the theft and the murder, though I didn’t consent to it. That’s why I needed your consent, so that you couldn’t have cornered me afterward, for what proof could you have had? I could always have cornered you, by revealing how eager you were for your father’s death, and I tell you, the public would have believed it all, and you’d have been ashamed for the rest of your life.”
“Was I really so eager? Was I?” Ivan snarled again.

“Of course you were, and by your consent you silently approved my doing it.” Smerdyakov looked resolutely at Ivan. He was very weak and spoke slowly and wearily, but some hidden inner force drove him on. He evidently had some purpose. Ivan sensed that.
